opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about Canvas is that it's really about moving beyond the pure chat paradigm. Chat is great for quick back-and-forth, but when you're actually working on something, whether that's an essay, a blog post, or a piece of code, you want a persistent artifact that you and the model are both looking at and editing together. You don't want to scroll up through twenty messages to find the latest version of your draft.

So the core idea was: what does it look like for the model to be a collaborator rather than just a responder? And writing and coding turned out to share a surprising amount of structure there. In both cases you have a document, you want targeted edits rather than full rewrites, you want to be able to highlight a section and say "make this tighter" or "fix this bug," and you want the model to understand the whole context of what you're building.

On the writing side, we thought a lot about things like adjusting length, changing reading level, adding final polish, or leaving inline comments and suggestions the way a good editor would. On the coding side, it's things like code review, adding logs, adding comments, porting to another language, fixing bugs. The shortcuts are different, but the underlying interaction is the same: the model needs to decide when to make a small, surgical edit versus when to rewrite something entirely, and when to just comment instead of touching your work at all.

A lot of the interesting research work was actually in training the model to make those judgment calls well. Like, when should it even open a canvas? If someone asks a quick question, you don't want this big side panel popping up. But if they say "help me write a cover letter," that's clearly an artifact. Getting that triggering behavior right, and getting the model to do targeted edits without breaking things, was a big part of it. We leaned heavily on synthetic data and evals for those specific behaviors.

And longer term, I think of Canvas as an early step toward models being genuine co-creators. The interface shapes what people think is possible with the model. If all you've ever seen is a chat box, you think of AI as something you ask questions to. If you see it working alongside you in a document, you start thinking of it as a teammate, and I think that shift in mental model matters a lot for where these products are going.

r001.rationale: The response says Canvas should open for artifact-oriented requests like writing a cover letter but not for quick questions, describing interface behavior that adapts to inferred intent.

r002.rationale: The response says writing and coding share the same underlying interaction, with different shortcuts; it does not characterize them as essentially different UIs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame Canvas is that it came out of a pretty simple observation: the chat interface is great for a lot of things, but it's actually a pretty bad surface for anything where you're iterating on an artifact. If you're writing an essay or writing code, the thing you care about isn't the conversation, it's the document. And in a chat, every time you ask for a change, the model regenerates the whole thing, it scrolls off the screen, you lose your place, you're copy-pasting back and forth. It felt like we were forcing a collaborative workflow through a text-messaging metaphor.

So Canvas is really about separating the conversation from the artifact. The chat is on one side, the thing you're actually making is on the other, and they talk to each other. You can highlight a paragraph and say "make this tighter," or select a function and say "add error handling here," and the model edits just that region instead of rewriting everything. That sounds small, but it changes the feel entirely. It stops being "ask the oracle" and starts being "work next to a collaborator who can see what I'm looking at."

For writing and coding specifically, I think they're more similar than people assume. In both cases you're going from a rough draft to something polished, and most of the work is in the revision, not the first pass. The difference is mostly in the kinds of shortcuts you want. For writing, it's things like adjusting length, changing reading level, adding polish, suggesting edits inline the way an editor would with comments in the margin. For code, it's reviewing, adding comments, fixing bugs, porting to another language, running it and seeing what breaks. So the shell is shared, but the affordances are tuned to the medium.

The hardest part, honestly, was the behavior side rather than the UI. We had to teach the model when to open a canvas at all. If you ask a quick question, you don't want a document popping up. If you say "help me draft a blog post," you probably do. And then once it's open, it has to decide: should I rewrite the whole thing or make a targeted edit? Early on it would over-trigger, or it would make a full rewrite when you wanted a one-line change, and that's really annoying. A lot of the work was synthetic data and evals to get those judgment calls right, because it's a taste problem more than a capability problem.

And I think the bigger picture is that this is one step toward interfaces where the model is more of a participant in your workspace than a chatbot you summon. Chat was the first form factor, but I don't think it's the last one.

r001.rationale: It says Canvas should open for requests like drafting a blog post but stay closed for quick questions, making the interface respond to inferred intent.

r002.rationale: It describes writing and coding as sharing a shell, with different affordances for each medium; it does not characterize them as essentially two different UIs.

astra-6.text:
I think of Canvas as a space where you and the model can work on the same thing. In a chat interface, you’re exchanging messages, but with writing or coding, there’s usually an artifact that you want to keep refining. Having that artifact alongside the conversation makes the interaction feel much more direct.

Writing and coding share that pattern. You might want feedback on the whole document or program, but you might also want to select one paragraph or one function and say, “Help me improve this.” The interface should make it easy to move between those levels without having to explain the context again.

The interesting design question is how much the model should do. Sometimes you want it to make an edit; sometimes you want a suggestion so you can decide. For me, the opportunity is to make that collaboration fluid while keeping the user in control of the work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses moving between document-level and selected-section work and choosing between edits and suggestions, but it does not say the interface should adapt to inferred user intent.

r002.rationale: The response presents writing and coding as sharing the same collaboration pattern; it does not characterize them as two different UIs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Canvas as a space where you can work with ChatGPT on an artifact, whether that’s a piece of writing or a piece of code. In a chat interface, you describe what you want, get a response, and then describe what you want to change. With Canvas, you can point directly to the part you’re working on and say, “Make this clearer,” or, “Help me understand this function.” You have a shared context for the collaboration.

Writing and coding both involve a lot of iteration. Sometimes you want the model to generate something, sometimes you want feedback, and sometimes you want a very specific edit while keeping everything else intact. The interface should make it easy to move between those modes and give you control over how much help you want.

r001.rationale: The response says the interface should support different collaboration modes and give users control over the amount of help, but it does not say the interface should adapt to inferred user intent.

r002.rationale: The response presents Canvas as a shared space for writing and code, not as two essentially different interfaces under one product name.
